powerRankings.blurb: It’s fair to wonder if a softer schedule over the last two weeks has aided the 49ers, and if their litany of injuries will be too much to overcome against better opponents. As of now, though, San Francisco boasts an offense that has cruise control set five miles per hour over the speed limit and is rolling along down the fast lane. Collectively, this team is strong enough to take care of business on a weekly basis. Oh, and those Brock Purdy MVP murmurs are legitimate, too.

The Chiefs are very aware of who they are just three weeks into the season. They didn't need to fully exert themselves on Sunday, earning a professional win against a scrappy but undermanned Dolphins team. They decreased Kenneth Walker III’s touches, too, which was a requirement for me in such a matchup, especially with most of the season still ahead.

After looking like a juggernaut through two weeks, the Bills did everything in their power to hand the Chargers a victory on Sunday. And yet, Josh Allen and Co. ultimately still won. Buffalo has plenty to clean up and can’t afford such a showing against the league’s best, but it’s telling when a team can look like a complete mess and still figure it out in time to prevail.

Sam Darnold’s first game back began with the most predictable outcome in the NFC West: a Jaxon Smith-Njigba touchdown reception. The rest was far from foreseeable. Two Darnold interceptions -- including a fourth-quarter pick-six -- doomed the Seahawks, who gave the Commanders a collection of extra chances and paid the price. No, that’s not a pun intended to demean rookie running back Jadarian Price (who fumbled early in the game and was benched for a while), although he didn’t help matters, either.

The Ravens returned closer to their explosive Week 1 form on Sunday, pulling off a thrilling win in Rio by executing slightly better than their opponent. They also have serious offensive issues in the red zone, but it was nice to see their passing attack open up again, thanks to the return of Zay Flowers.

Eventually, the Broncos will play a complete game. For now, we’ll have to accept that their defense is going to hold long enough for their offense to wake up in most weeks (and is liable to make a few game-changing plays in every contest, especially in the second half) and acknowledge that their big-time offensive playmakers still make this a better unit than it was a year ago.

What a nice get-right week for the Jaguars, who handled the Patriots with ease and even tousled their hair for good measure. Congratulations are in order for Travis Hunter, who recorded his first career interception amid a runaway win for Jacksonville.

Cincinnati's hyped defense took a big reputation hit Sunday when it allowed Aaron Rodgers to turn back the clock and lead Pittsburgh -- the NFL’s second-worst scoring offense entering Week 3 -- to a 30-point performance and a one-score win over a division rival. It’s tough to pin down exactly where the Bengals stand after a loss like this, but I think we’ll learn plenty in this week’s cats-vs.-cats showdown with the Jaguars.

I know the Vikings' offense is completely unreliable. I also know Minnesota’s defense is special and the reason these Vikes are 3-0. That’s enough for me to move them into the top 10 for the first time this season, even if I still can’t trust Kyler Murray.

Sure, I might be overreacting to the Raiders’ hot start, but how can I pass on the rare opportunity to push the Silver and Black into the top 10? Klint Kubiak has inspired this previously downtrodden franchise, and Las Vegas is playing a wildly entertaining brand of football built on contributions from both established (Kirk Cousins, Brock Bowers) and unknown players (fifth-round rookie Hezekiah Masses has three interceptions this season!).

Dallas could have scored a major victory in an international setting if coach Brian Schottenheimer hadn’t micromanaged the end-game situation with an underlying fear of defeat powering his decisions. There were plenty of positives in this game, though: The Cowboys' maligned defense finally earned a signature stop with a goal-line stand that opened the door for a fourth-quarter comeback, Dak Prescott continued to play at an elite level with both CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, and rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham logged the first significant stop of his pro career. The same problems surfaced in the end, though, when the defense allowed the Ravens to complete a deep pass to set up a walk-off field goal that never should have been on the table in the game’s final second. I suppose it’s a good lesson to learn in the first month of the season.

Who needs Caleb Williams when you have ... Case Keenum?! Monday night served as a testament to the value of experience and lasting athletic talent, because they blended perfectly to produce a memorable performance for Keenum, the 38-year-old who diced up the Eagles and propelled Chicago’s offense to a 20-point victory. As impressive as Keenum was, so too was Chicago’s defense, which stifled Philadelphia’s offense, forced three turnovers and ensured the Eagles weren’t going to come close to mounting a comeback. It’s only one win, but it represents a whole lot more for the Bears, who had every reason to lose themselves in self-pity. They instead decided to rise above and drop a hammer on Philadelphia.

We’ve seen the Rams look flat (20-point loss to the 49ers in Australia), play like an elite team (22-point win over the Giants in Los Angeles) and collapse in a road game they led 16-0 at halftime (Sunday night's defeat to the Broncos). It’s better to get these mistakes out of the way now, but we can all agree this isn’t how we expected L.A. to start its season.

We know the Lions can put up points in bunches by leaning heavily on Jahmyr Gibbs, and this offense is capable of keeping them in every game they play. Their defensive struggles in the fourth quarter remain concerning, even if a takeaway saved them from another trip to overtime.

The Eagles failed their first real test of 2026 in a fashion that suggested they didn’t even take time to study. Jalen Hurts struggled for most of the night, Philadelphia wasted a promising, Saquon Barkley-heavy drive by throwing an interception in the end zone, and the defense surrendered 375 yards to a Case Keenum-led offense. The Eagles’ offensive evolution under Sean Mannion hasn’t yet taken hold (Hurts didn’t help with that much on Monday night), and right now, I’m not exactly sure how to feel about this team. Philly should be good, but through three weeks, it has logged two narrow wins over teams it's expected to beat, and lost a lopsided game on the road. Not great, Nick (Sirianni)!

Instead of putting it all together in the fourth quarter as they had in their first two games, the Saints inverted on Sunday, falling apart in spectacular fashion in a loss to the Raiders. Tyler Shough’s fourth-quarter clutch gene disappeared in a wild game that should serve as a bit of humble pie for an upstart team that could benefit from such a lesson in late September.

The Browns’ defense is back and playing a cohesive brand that rivals the best units in the NFL over the last two weeks. Mason Graham is off to a fantastic start, Jared Verse has started to make an impact and Carson Schwesinger picked up right where he left off in last season's Defensive Rookie of the Year campaign. Deshaun Watson also seems to have rediscovered a fourth-quarter clutch mode we haven’t seen from him since he was in Houston. Cleveland's offense needs to be better, but the Browns have definitely looked competent and earned the last two wins.

I don’t believe in moral victories, but I do think teams can find positives in close losses. After the Week 2 nightmare at MetLife Stadium, the Jets had plenty to be proud of in Sunday's road defeat. Sure, they gave up 31 to Detroit (just like the last two defenses that faced the Lions), but they battled back from a two-touchdown deficit in the fourth quarter to give themselves a legitimate chance to win in the Motor City. That’s much, much more than we could have said about the Jets in recent years.

Pittsburgh's offense woke up! It was refreshing to watch the Steelers finally produce with the approach (aggressively pushing the ball downfield) they’ve been trying to force this season. It wasn’t at all surprising that their defense was the one to finish the job, either. I won’t be taken for an easy sale, though; they’ll need to do it more than once offensively for me to emotionally invest.

In what was the toughest watch of the week, the Colts managed to outlast the Texans despite three Daniel Jones giveaways. They can thank their defense -- one of the worst in the NFL entering Week 3 -- for finding some solid footing and shutting down Houston's woeful offense (for most of the game). Kicker Spencer Shrader deserves some flowers, too, because the guy has been nails this season: 8-for-8 on field-goal attempts, including 3-for-3 from 50-plus.

Marcus Mariota hive, stand up! The veteran backup played hero Sunday, powering Washington past Seattle for the biggest upset of the week. The contest ended in fitting fashion with Mariota scrambling for the game-sealing first down. Equal praise is due for Washington's defense, which has played above expectation all season and notched a peak showing in the takeaways department, logging two to keep the Commanders in the game and a third to give them enough of a lead to emerge victorious.

Last week’s drubbing of Atlanta appeared to be an anomaly by the time Sunday’s game concluded. Carolina’s offense struggled to find success for most of the afternoon in Cleveland, a reality exacerbated by the injury to Jalen Coker. Devin Lloyd’s absence hurt the Panthers’ defense, which wilted in the fourth quarter against a motivated Browns offense. Carolina also struggled to protect Bryce Young, who was banged up and saw his performance suffer because of it. Fortunately, the bye week is near, but not before a Sunday night date with the Lions that could teach us plenty about the current state of the Panthers.

With their backs against the wall, the Falcons traveled to Green Bay with renewed energy and benefitted from the contributions of one of the NFL’s best players in Bijan Robinson, an elite playmaker who shines brightest under the prime-time lights. HC Kevin Stefanski and OC Tommy Rees didn’t get too cute in their first game with Michael Penix Jr. in the lineup, leaning heavily on Robinson and allowing their star running back to open up the rest of the offense in a lopsided victory that repaired the Falcons' reputation and may have saved their season.

The Texans have serious problems offensively that are painfully familiar. They can’t run the ball, lack difference-makers at receiver and still can’t consistently sustain drives. After a six-point output in the Week 2 loss to Cincinnati, the Texans were nearly as dreadful Sunday in Indianapolis, save for one urgent drive to briefly take a late lead. It’s unrealistic to expect the defense to carry Houston on a weekly basis, and until offensive coordinator Nick Caley finds some solutions, the Texans will remain mired in these struggles.

We shouldn’t be surprised the Giants traded for J.J. McCarthy on Monday, not after that rough showing from their offense vs. Tennessee amid a downpour at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. We also shouldn't be surprised the Giants won an ugly game. It’s precisely the type of contest John Harbaugh’s team is built to win. How New York proceeds from here -- including how quickly McCarthy sees the field -- is hard to say, making this 2-1 team one of the biggest wild cards in the NFL.

I’ll give credit to the Cardinals for refusing to quit Sunday in a game in which lesser teams would have laid down and accepted defeat. There is still plenty to clean up, especially for a defense that gave up a ton of big plays to the 49ers.

The Chargers fixed many errors in the first half against the Bills on Sunday, playing a clean two quarters that included three takeaways. Signs of an impending loss were still evident, though, as Los Angeles only scored 10 points off those turnovers before reverting to its sloppy ways in the second half, crumbling and giving away a very winnable game on the road. I understand your frustration, Chargers fans.

Matt LaFleur accurately summarized Thursday's 21-point loss to Atlanta in the postgame interview, calling it a “humbling night.” Green Bay’s offense lacks a running game and is putting too much on the shoulders of Jordan Love, and the defense’s inability to tackle effectively doomed the Packers in their second defeat. It’s fair to say they could easily be 0-3 right now, and I’m not sure where they go from here. If these issues persist against the Buccaneers in Week 4, we’ll be entering crisis territory.

Tampa Bay’s offense remains stuck in the mud. It can’t protect Baker Mayfield, who also can’t find much comfort in Zac Robinson’s offense, which lacks a clear direction. This roster is good enough to be better than 0-3, yet that’s what these Bucs are after three weeks. And now they're facing a disaster scenario, with Mayfield expected to miss at least three weeks due to the thumb injury he suffered at the end of Sunday’s disheartening loss.

The Dolphins perform admirably between the 20-yard lines on a weekly basis but can’t find ways to finish drives with trips to the end zone. They’re the most undermanned team in the NFL but don’t lack effort. In this league, however, talent tends to win when effort is comparable. For now, Miami is still figuring out how to walk before attempting to run.

Save for the defensively driven victory in Week 2, the Patriots have been a mess and have a major problem at quarterback. Drake Maye looks completely lost, and judging by the tone of his postgame press conference on Sunday, he might not find his way back onto New England's intended route for some time. Mike Vrabel was right when describing his concern level as “very high” afterward. There are problems everywhere for the defending AFC champions and a simple solution isn’t in sight.

A second straight rainy Sunday at MetLife Stadium claimed the Titans’ offense as its victim. Tennessee finally found some life late in its Week 3 loss to the Giants, but Cam Ward -- who has experienced a rough start to his sophomore season -- made a horrendous decision, throwing an end zone interception to a lurking Jevon Holland to seal another defeat. Tennessee is currently on a one step forward, two steps back pacing that doesn’t lead me to believe it'll suddenly improve any time soon.
